topic:
Research question: Are there more color pigments to discover?
Context: It is possible to create new pigments, but not new colors. The first synthetic pigment was made in the early 1700s. In 2009, chemist Mas Subramanian accidently created a new blue pigment called “YInMn Blue.”

ideas.title: Latent Defect-Optical Surrogates for Discovering High-NIR Red Mn/Cr Oxide Pigments
ideas.motivation: The original query asks whether more color pigments can be discovered. The answer is yes if new pigment materials, not new perceptual color categories, are found by design. Red Mn-oxide and Cr-doped oxide systems already show that visible red color can be coupled to near-infrared reflectance [Gramm et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1002/zaac.202000274) [Divya et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2021.07.218) [Liu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2025.08.005), and the YInMn-blue case shows that unusual local coordination can create intense pigment color [Ransmayr et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevmaterials.6.105003). The remaining bottleneck is predictive: pigment discovery is still empirical because local coordination, defect states, electronic transitions, powder scattering, and NIR loss are not jointly modeled. This idea transfers surrogate hidden representations from data-efficient predictive chemistry [Chen et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00256g) and physics-informed machine learning for chemical systems [Keith et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.1c00107) to pigment science. Instead of a generic defect similarity score, the method learns a hidden latent representation from physically assignable defect-loss optical channels, enabling controlled discovery of new high-NIR red pigment variants.
ideas.methods: 1. Fixed-hue defect library with morphology and phase controls: Use Li2MnO3 as the primary red host because it is a rare Mn4+ red oxide and a NIR-reflective pigment target [Gramm et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1002/zaac.202000274). Prepare one phase-pure batch, then split it into aliquots and anneal at the same temperature and time under different oxygen partial pressures. This varies only the oxygen-vacancy and Mn3+/Mn4+ defect population. Thermal treatment is known to alter local transition-metal environments and color in Mn-doped oxides [Oshita et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.35848/1347-4065/ad17e0). Particle morphology and powder scattering are controlled by milling, sieving, and imaging, because pigment color depends on morphology and scattering [Splinter et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules29153527) [Ransmayr et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevmaterials.6.105003). CIELAB hue angle and color contrast are used to define a fixed-hue acceptance window [Ferro et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.omx.2022.100167). 2. Physically assignable defect-loss decomposition: Convert diffuse reflectance to Kubelka-Munk absorption and fit the visible-NIR spectrum as a sum of mechanistic loss channels: Mn4+ d-d transitions, Mn3+/Mn4+ intervalence charge transfer, oxygen-vacancy polaron absorption, and a free-carrier or broad NIR tail; for Cr-containing candidates add Cr3+ site-distortion transitions [Ransmayr et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevmaterials.6.105003) [Liu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2025.08.005). The spectral fit is constrained by XPS, XAS, and EPR quantification of Mn valence and defect proxies, so the channels represent causal defect states rather than generic descriptors. This decomposition directly addresses the need to move from broad defect similarity to assignable loss mechanisms in red NIR pigments [Gramm et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1002/zaac.202000274). 3. Latent defect-optical surrogate: Borrow the surrogate hidden representation mechanism from data-efficient predictive chemistry [Chen et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00256g). Train a surrogate model first to predict the defect-loss channel vector from physics-informed inputs, then use its hidden layer as a latent defect-optical representation for downstream prediction of fixed-hue NIR reflectance and hue stability. Inputs include composition, oxidation state, polyhedral distortion, bond distance, vacancy formation propensity, and transition energy, following hybrid machine-learning and computational-chemistry practice [Keith et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.1c00107). Baselines and controls include composition-only, explicit-descriptor-only, defect-channel-only linear models, unstructured feature concatenation, and randomized latent features or shuffled channel labels, with model capacity and data splits held fixed. 4. Mechanistic applicability domain and discovery loop: Define an applicability domain using polyhedral distortion, vacancy formation propensity, transition-energy overlap, and defect-loss channel similarity, not merely composition distance. Screen known red and orange Mn/Cr oxide hosts and variants, including Li3AlMnO5 [Divya et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2021.07.218), La3LiMnO7 [Oka et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules26206243), and Cr-doped LaAlO3 [Liu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2025.08.005). Select high-ranking in-domain candidates and matched out-of-domain or random candidates as controls. Synthesize and measure all candidates with the same powder standard to test whether the latent defect-optical model discovers new high-NIR pigment variants rather than merely fitting known compositions. Use these to assign Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio and oxygen-vacancy-related states.; Perform Kubelka-Munk analysis to separate absorption from scattering. Reject or statistically control any sample whose scattering coefficient or particle-size distribution changed, ruling out morphology as the cause of NIR changes.; Decompose absorption into the predefined defect-loss channels and test the physical causal relation by mediation analysis: oxygen partial pressure affects defect channel intensity, which affects NIR reflectance, while hue and scattering are held fixed. If the effect disappears after controlling for defect channel intensity, the defect channel is the causal variable.; Primary one-factor model test: using the same controlled dataset, train the latent defect-optical surrogate and all baselines. Hold data splits, model size, optimizer, and evaluation metric fixed; vary only representation type: latent defect-optical hidden state, composition-only, explicit-descriptor-only, defect-channel-only, unstructured concatenation, and randomized latent features or shuffled channel labels.; Evaluate the primary hypothesis by held-out MAE and rank correlation for NIR reflectance at fixed hue. The latent defect-optical representation must outperform composition-only, explicit-descriptor-only, unstructured mixture, and randomized controls under paired cross-validation to be accepted.; Apply the mechanistic applicability domain to screen secondary hosts and processing states: Na/Ti-substituted Li2MnO3, Li3AlMnO5, La3LiMnO7, and Cr-doped LaAlO3. Select three high-ranking in-domain candidates and three matched out-of-domain or random candidates as controls.; Synthesize and anneal the selected candidates with the same phase, particle-size, and reflectance protocol. Confirm that in-domain candidates give higher NIR reflectance at comparable hue and that the improvement correlates with predicted defect-loss suppression, not with particle size, phase impurity, or composition alone. Only after this pass, expand to broader hosts, sustainability feedstocks, or thermochromic variants.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the lack of a predictive, defect-specific route to new high-NIR red oxide pigments; it can be divided into 4 parts: (1) a fixed-hue, morphology-controlled defect library, (2) decomposition of optical loss into physically assignable defect channels, (3) a latent defect-optical surrogate whose hidden representation is trained on those channels, and (4) a mechanistic applicability domain for selecting new pigment variants. The primary testable hypothesis is that a hidden representation trained to reconstruct defect-specific loss channels predicts fixed-hue NIR reflectance changes caused by controlled defect populations more accurately than composition-only or explicit-descriptor models, and that this improvement is not explained by particle scattering, phase impurity, or composition alone.

proposed_method.name: Fixed-hue defect library with morphology and phase controls
proposed_method.description: Use Li2MnO3 as the primary red host because it is a rare Mn4+ red oxide and a NIR-reflective pigment target [Gramm et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1002/zaac.202000274). Prepare one phase-pure batch, then split it into aliquots and anneal at the same temperature and time under different oxygen partial pressures. This varies only the oxygen-vacancy and Mn3+/Mn4+ defect population. Thermal treatment is known to alter local transition-metal environments and color in Mn-doped oxides [Oshita et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.35848/1347-4065/ad17e0). Particle morphology and powder scattering are controlled by milling, sieving, and imaging, because pigment color depends on morphology and scattering [Splinter et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules29153527) [Ransmayr et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevmaterials.6.105003). CIELAB hue angle and color contrast are used to define a fixed-hue acceptance window [Ferro et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.omx.2022.100167).

proposed_method.name: Physically assignable defect-loss decomposition
proposed_method.description: Convert diffuse reflectance to Kubelka-Munk absorption and fit the visible-NIR spectrum as a sum of mechanistic loss channels: Mn4+ d-d transitions, Mn3+/Mn4+ intervalence charge transfer, oxygen-vacancy polaron absorption, and a free-carrier or broad NIR tail; for Cr-containing candidates add Cr3+ site-distortion transitions [Ransmayr et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevmaterials.6.105003) [Liu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2025.08.005). The spectral fit is constrained by XPS, XAS, and EPR quantification of Mn valence and defect proxies, so the channels represent causal defect states rather than generic descriptors. This decomposition directly addresses the need to move from broad defect similarity to assignable loss mechanisms in red NIR pigments [Gramm et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1002/zaac.202000274).

proposed_method.name: Latent defect-optical surrogate
proposed_method.description: Borrow the surrogate hidden representation mechanism from data-efficient predictive chemistry [Chen et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00256g). Train a surrogate model first to predict the defect-loss channel vector from physics-informed inputs, then use its hidden layer as a latent defect-optical representation for downstream prediction of fixed-hue NIR reflectance and hue stability. Inputs include composition, oxidation state, polyhedral distortion, bond distance, vacancy formation propensity, and transition energy, following hybrid machine-learning and computational-chemistry practice [Keith et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.1c00107). Baselines and controls include composition-only, explicit-descriptor-only, defect-channel-only linear models, unstructured feature concatenation, and randomized latent features or shuffled channel labels, with model capacity and data splits held fixed.

proposed_method.name: Mechanistic applicability domain and discovery loop
proposed_method.description: Define an applicability domain using polyhedral distortion, vacancy formation propensity, transition-energy overlap, and defect-loss channel similarity, not merely composition distance. Screen known red and orange Mn/Cr oxide hosts and variants, including Li3AlMnO5 [Divya et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2021.07.218), La3LiMnO7 [Oka et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules26206243), and Cr-doped LaAlO3 [Liu et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ceramint.2025.08.005). Select high-ranking in-domain candidates and matched out-of-domain or random candidates as controls. Synthesize and measure all candidates with the same powder standard to test whether the latent defect-optical model discovers new high-NIR pigment variants rather than merely fitting known compositions.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Harnessing surrogate models for data-efficient predictive chemistry: descriptors vs. learned hidden representations
analogy_mapping.concept: Surrogate models trained on scarce chemistry data can produce hidden representations that are more transferable than explicit predicted descriptors.
analogy_mapping.adaptation: The pigment surrogate is trained to reconstruct physically assignable defect-loss optical channels; its hidden layer becomes a latent defect-optical representation used to predict fixed-hue NIR reflectance and prioritize new red pigment variants.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Combining Machine Learning and Computational Chemistry for Predictive Insights Into Chemical Systems
analogy_mapping.concept: Machine learning becomes more predictive when coupled with physics-informed chemical descriptors and iterative computational/experimental feedback.
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Pigment inputs are encoded as mechanistic descriptors such as oxidation state, polyhedral distortion, vacancy formation propensity, and transition energy, and the model is cycled against controlled annealing experiments and optical modeling.

experiment_plan: Phase 0 materials standard: synthesize one large batch of phase-pure Li2MnO3, confirm single phase by XRD/Rietveld, mill and sieve to a fixed particle-size window, and record HIM/SEM morphology and BET surface area. This batch is the only source for the primary controlled experiment, so composition and morphology are held fixed.

Split the batch into five aliquots and anneal at identical temperature and time under different oxygen partial pressures, then quench. The only varied physical factor is oxygen defect population. Include an air-annealed replicate and a physical mixture of the most oxidized and most reduced powders to test linear mixing and scattering effects.

Measure packed-powder CIELAB, hue angle, solar reflectance, and UV-vis-NIR diffuse reflectance using identical sample thickness and geometry. Retain for primary analysis only samples inside a pre-registered fixed-hue window, or include hue angle as a covariate; this keeps the target fixed-hue NIR reflectance.
Quantify defect proxies on each aliquot: Mn 3s/2p XPS, Mn K-edge XAS, EPR, and chemical titration if feasible. Use these to assign Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio and oxygen-vacancy-related states.

Perform Kubelka-Munk analysis to separate absorption from scattering. Reject or statistically control any sample whose scattering coefficient or particle-size distribution changed, ruling out morphology as the cause of NIR changes.

Decompose absorption into the predefined defect-loss channels and test the physical causal relation by mediation analysis: oxygen partial pressure affects defect channel intensity, which affects NIR reflectance, while hue and scattering are held fixed. If the effect disappears after controlling for defect channel intensity, the defect channel is the causal variable.

Primary one-factor model test: using the same controlled dataset, train the latent defect-optical surrogate and all baselines. Hold data splits, model size, optimizer, and evaluation metric fixed; vary only representation type: latent defect-optical hidden state, composition-only, explicit-descriptor-only, defect-channel-only, unstructured concatenation, and randomized latent features or shuffled channel labels.

Evaluate the primary hypothesis by held-out MAE and rank correlation for NIR reflectance at fixed hue. The latent defect-optical representation must outperform composition-only, explicit-descriptor-only, unstructured mixture, and randomized controls under paired cross-validation to be accepted.

Apply the mechanistic applicability domain to screen secondary hosts and processing states: Na/Ti-substituted Li2MnO3, Li3AlMnO5, La3LiMnO7, and Cr-doped LaAlO3. Select three high-ranking in-domain candidates and three matched out-of-domain or random candidates as controls.

Synthesize and anneal the selected candidates with the same phase, particle-size, and reflectance protocol. Confirm that in-domain candidates give higher NIR reflectance at comparable hue and that the improvement correlates with predicted defect-loss suppression, not with particle size, phase impurity, or composition alone. Only after this pass, expand to broader hosts, sustainability feedstocks, or thermochromic variants.

ideas.novelty_justification: The closest existing combination is the Li2MnO3 high-NIR red pigment work plus Cr3+-doped LaAlO3 red/NIR pigment work, reinforced by YInMn structure-optical/thermochromic studies and morphology/scattering references. Those references already establish the target materials, the red/NIR property goal, and the relevance of local coordination, defects/valence, and particle morphology. The proposal adds a fixed-host, fixed-morphology oxygen-defect experiment; Kubelka-Munk decomposition into physically assigned defect-loss channels constrained by XPS/XAS/EPR; and a surrogate hidden representation trained on those channels to predict fixed-hue NIR reflectance and screen candidates. This specific defect-channel latent surrogate and causal mediation/applicability-domain framework is not disclosed by the cited references and is a testable conceptual addition. However, the advance is mainly an integration of known pigment hosts, spectroscopic decomposition, defect characterization, and latent-representation ML rather than a wholly new mechanism; the core problem and ingredients are already present in the references. Thus it is more than low but not high, and the combination-oriented nature caps it at medium.
improvement_suggestions: Sharpen the mechanistic claim from 'a latent representation helps prediction' to 'a low-dimensional, causally identifiable defect-loss coordinate is the minimal sufficient mediator of NIR loss at fixed hue.' Define that coordinate, for example as integrated oscillator strength of Mn3+/Mn4+ intervalence plus oxygen-vacancy polaron absorption, and validate it through interventions such as pO2 annealing, aliovalent substitution, or vacancy trapping, while testing invariance across hosts.

Introduce a hue-NIR decoupling principle or metric, such as fixed-hue NIR efficiency defined as scattering-corrected NIR reflectance per unit visible hue strength, and show the latent defect-optical model can optimize this metric by suppressing only the NIR-loss channel while preserving the hue-producing transition. Make transferability a conceptual test: require the learned defect-optical manifold to predict out-of-sample hosts only when channel labels and physical constraints are preserved, and demonstrate that a universal defect-loss manifold transfers between Mn and Cr hosts despite different compositions.
